nodes.statement: A \emph{weak \( \beta \)-specification} is a triple \( W = (R^\Atom, R^\NearLitter, \sigma) \) where \( R^\Atom, R^\NearLitter \) are \( \beta \)-trees of relations on \( \kappa \), and \( \sigma \) is a \( \beta \)-specification. We say that a weak specification \emph{specifies} a support \( S \) if there is a strong support \( T \) such that \( \sigma = \spec(T) \), \( S \preceq T \), and \begin{align*} (i, j) \in R_A^\Atom &\leftrightarrow \exists a,\, (i, a) \in S_A^\Atom \wedge (j, a) \in T_A^\Atom \\ (i, j) \in R_A^\NearLitter &\leftrightarrow \exists N,\, (i, N) \in S_A^\NearLitter \wedge (j, N) \in T_A^\NearLitter \end{align*}
nodes.name: weak specification
nodes.statement_short: A weak specification: relation trees plus a specification, specifying supports that embed into a strong support with that specification.
nodes.label: def:WeakSpec

nodes.statement: Every support has a weak specification that specifies it.
nodes.name: exists_weakSpec
conclusions: Every support has a weak specification that specifies it.
nodes.label: prop:exists_weakSpec

nodes.statement: Let \( S \) be a support, and let \( T \) be a strong support such that \( S \preceq T \), which exists by \cref{prop:exists_strong}. Then simply define \( R^\Atom \) and \( R^\NearLitter \) to be the required relations.
nodes.name: Proof of exists_weakSpec
nodes.statement_short: Take a strong extension and read off the relations.

nodes.statement: If \( W \) is a weak specification that specifies supports \( S \) and \( T \), then there is an allowable permutation \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(S) = T \).
nodes.name: exists_allowable_of_weakSpec
assumptions: \( W \) is a weak specification that specifies supports \( S \) and \( T \)
conclusions: there is an allowable permutation \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(S) = T \)
nodes.label: prop:exists_allowable_of_weakSpec

nodes.statement: Let \( W = (R^\Atom, R^\NearLitter, \sigma) \), and let \( U, V \) be strong supports such that \( \spec(U) = \sigma = \spec(V) \), \( S \preceq U, T \preceq V \), and \begin{align*} (\exists a,\, (i, a) \in S_A^\Atom \wedge (j, a) \in U_A^\Atom) &\leftrightarrow (\exists a,\, (i, a) \in T_A^\Atom \wedge (j, a) \in V_A^\Atom) \\ (\exists N,\, (i, N) \in S_A^\NearLitter \wedge (j, N) \in U_A^\NearLitter) &\leftrightarrow (\exists N,\, (i, N) \in T_A^\NearLitter \wedge (j, N) \in V_A^\NearLitter) \end{align*} By \cref{prop:exists_allowable_of_spec_eq_spec}, there is an allowable permutation \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(U) = V \). We claim that \( \rho(S) = T \). Suppose \( (i, a) \in S_A^\Atom \). Then as \( S \preceq U \), there is \( j \) such that \( (j, a) \in U_A^\Atom \). So there is \( a' \) such that \( (i, a') \in T_A^\Atom \) and \( (j, a') \in V_A^\Atom \). Then \( a' = \rho_A(a) \) as \( \rho(U) = V \), as required. The same simple calculation gives the required result for near-litters.
nodes.name: Proof of exists_allowable_of_weakSpec
nodes.statement_short: Strong supports with equal specifications are related by an allowable permutation; the relation trees transport S to T.
Unfold the strong supports U, V.
nodes.statement: Let \( W = (R^\Atom, R^\NearLitter, \sigma) \), and let \( U, V \) be strong supports such that \( \spec(U) = \sigma = \spec(V) \), \( S \preceq U, T \preceq V \), and \begin{align*} (\exists a,\, (i, a) \in S_A^\Atom \wedge (j, a) \in U_A^\Atom) &\leftrightarrow (\exists a,\, (i, a) \in T_A^\Atom \wedge (j, a) \in V_A^\Atom) \\ (\exists N,\, (i, N) \in S_A^\NearLitter \wedge (j, N) \in U_A^\NearLitter) &\leftrightarrow (\exists N,\, (i, N) \in T_A^\NearLitter \wedge (j, N) \in V_A^\NearLitter) \end{align*}
nodes.name: Unfold the strong supports U, V

nodes.statement_short: Get rho with rho(U) = V.
nodes.statement: By \cref{prop:exists_allowable_of_spec_eq_spec}, there is an allowable permutation \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(U) = V \).
nodes.name: Get rho with rho(U) = V

nodes.statement_short: rho maps S to T.
nodes.statement: We claim that \( \rho(S) = T \). Suppose \( (i, a) \in S_A^\Atom \). Then as \( S \preceq U \), there is \( j \) such that \( (j, a) \in U_A^\Atom \). So there is \( a' \) such that \( (i, a') \in T_A^\Atom \) and \( (j, a') \in V_A^\Atom \). Then \( a' = \rho_A(a) \) as \( \rho(U) = V \), as required. The same simple calculation gives the required result for near-litters.
nodes.name: rho maps S to T

nodes.statement_short: Index a in U.
nodes.statement: Suppose \( (i, a) \in S_A^\Atom \). Then as \( S \preceq U \), there is \( j \) such that \( (j, a) \in U_A^\Atom \).
nodes.name: Index a in U

nodes.statement_short: a' = rho_A(a); same for near-litters.
nodes.statement: So there is \( a' \) such that \( (i, a') \in T_A^\Atom \) and \( (j, a') \in V_A^\Atom \). Then \( a' = \rho_A(a) \) as \( \rho(U) = V \), as required. The same simple calculation gives the required result for near-litters.
nodes.name: a' = rho_A(a); same for near-litters

nodes.statement: Suppose that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions. Then there are less than \( \#\mu \) weak \( \beta \)-specifications.
nodes.name: card_weakSpec
assumptions: Suppose that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions.
conclusions: there are less than \( \#\mu \) weak \( \beta \)-specifications
nodes.label: prop:card_weakSpec

nodes.statement: Follows directly from \cref{prop:card_spec} and the remark that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-trees of relations on \( \kappa \).
nodes.name: Proof of card_weakSpec
nodes.statement_short: Specifications plus trees of relations.

nodes.statement: Suppose that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions. Then there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-support orbits.
nodes.name: card_supportOrbit
assumptions: Suppose that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions.
conclusions: there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-support orbits
nodes.label: prop:card_supportOrbit

nodes.statement: Define a function from the type of \( \beta \)-support orbits into the type of weak \( \beta \)-specifications by mapping a representative to a weak specification that specifies it; one will always exist by \cref{prop:exists_weakSpec}. This is an injection: if \( o_1, o_2 \) are orbits with representatives \( S_1, S_2 \) and \( S_1, S_2 \) have the same assigned weak specification, then by \cref{prop:exists_allowable_of_weakSpec} there is an allowable permutation \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(S_1) = S_2 \), and so \( o_1 = o_2 \). So we are done as there are less than \( \#\mu \) weak \( \beta \)-specifications by \cref{prop:card_weakSpec}.
nodes.name: Proof of card_supportOrbit
nodes.statement_short: Inject support orbits into weak specifications.
Assign each orbit a weak specification.
nodes.statement: Define a function from the type of \( \beta \)-support orbits into the type of weak \( \beta \)-specifications by mapping a representative to a weak specification that specifies it; one will always exist by \cref{prop:exists_weakSpec}.
nodes.name: Assign each orbit a weak specification

nodes.statement_short: Injective by exists_allowable_of_weakSpec.
nodes.statement: This is an injection: if \( o_1, o_2 \) are orbits with representatives \( S_1, S_2 \) and \( S_1, S_2 \) have the same assigned weak specification, then by \cref{prop:exists_allowable_of_weakSpec} there is an allowable permutation \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(S_1) = S_2 \), and so \( o_1 = o_2 \).
nodes.name: Injective by exists_allowable_of_weakSpec

nodes.statement_short: Bound by card_weakSpec.
nodes.statement: So we are done as there are less than \( \#\mu \) weak \( \beta \)-specifications by \cref{prop:card_weakSpec}.
nodes.name: Bound by card_weakSpec

nodes.statement: Let \( \beta \) be a type index (which in practice will be \( \bot \) or the lowest proper type index). Suppose that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-support orbits. Let \( \nu \) be a cardinal less than \( \#\mu \) such that for each \( \beta \)-support \( S \), there are at most \( \nu \)-many objects \( x : \TSet_\beta \) that \( S \) supports. Then there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-coding functions.
nodes.name: card_codingFunction_of_card_supports
assumptions: Let \( \beta \) be a type index (which in practice will be \( \bot \) or the lowest proper type index).
Suppose that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-support orbits.
Let \( \nu \) be a cardinal less than \( \#\mu \) such that for each \( \beta \)-support \( S \), there are at most \( \nu \)-many objects \( x : \TSet_\beta \) that \( S \) supports.
conclusions: there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-coding functions
nodes.label: prop:card_codingFunction_of_card_supports

nodes.statement: Every \( \beta \)-coding function is of the form \( \chi_{(x, S)} \) where \( S \) is a representative chosen in advance for a support orbit, and \( x \) is an object that \( S \) supports under the action of \( \beta \)-allowable permutations. So there are at most \[ \sum_{S \text{ representatives}} \nu = \#\{\text{support orbits}\} \cdot \nu \] coding functions, which is less than \( \#\mu \).
nodes.name: Proof of card_codingFunction_of_card_supports
nodes.statement_short: Count pairs of an orbit representative and a supported object.

nodes.statement: There are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \bot \)-coding functions.
nodes.name: card_codingFunction_bot
conclusions: There are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \bot \)-coding functions.
nodes.label: prop:card_codingFunction_bot

nodes.statement: By \cref{prop:card_codingFunction_of_card_supports}, it suffices to show that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \bot \)-support orbits and that there is a bound less than \( \#\mu \) on the amount of objects that a given \( \bot \)-support supports. The first result follows from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit}, which has vacuous assumptions in this case. The second result follows from applying \cref{prop:card_supports_atoms} to singletons of atoms, after applying the bijections between \( \bot \)-supports and base supports, and between \( \bot \)-allowable permutations and base permutations.
nodes.name: Proof of card_codingFunction_bot
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via card_codingFunction_of_card_supports; bound orbits and supported sets.
Reduce to two bounds.
nodes.statement: By \cref{prop:card_codingFunction_of_card_supports}, it suffices to show that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \bot \)-support orbits and that there is a bound less than \( \#\mu \) on the amount of objects that a given \( \bot \)-support supports.
nodes.name: Reduce to two bounds

nodes.statement_short: Orbits via card_supportOrbit.
nodes.statement: The first result follows from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit}, which has vacuous assumptions in this case.
nodes.name: Orbits via card_supportOrbit

nodes.statement_short: Supported sets via card_supports_atoms.
nodes.statement: The second result follows from applying \cref{prop:card_supports_atoms} to singletons of atoms, after applying the bijections between \( \bot \)-supports and base supports, and between \( \bot \)-allowable permutations and base permutations.
nodes.name: Supported sets via card_supports_atoms

nodes.statement: There are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-coding functions if \( \beta \) is the minimal inhabitant of \( \lambda \).
nodes.name: card_codingFunction_min
assumptions: \( \beta \) is the minimal inhabitant of \( \lambda \)
conclusions: There are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-coding functions
nodes.label: prop:card_codingFunction_min

nodes.statement: Again, we apply \cref{prop:card_codingFunction_of_card_supports}. The first claim follows from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit}, where this time we use the fact that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \bot \)-coding functions (\cref{prop:card_codingFunction_bot}). The second claim follows from \cref{prop:card_supports_atoms} to \( \bot \)-extensions of type \( \beta \) objects, noting that \( \beta \)-supports correspond to base supports and that \( \beta \)-allowable permutations correspond to base permutations.\footnote{One useful claim to prove for this is that there is a unique path \( \beta \tpath \bot \), and so type \( \beta \) objects satisfy \( \bot \)-extensionality by injectivity of \( U_\beta \).} The fact that \( \beta \)-allowable permutations correspond to base permutations relies on the fact that we can construct a \( \beta \)-permutation from a base permutation using coherent data (\cref{def:CoherentData}).
nodes.name: Proof of card_codingFunction_min
nodes.statement_short: As for the bottom case, using coherent data to identify beta-permutations with base permutations.
Reduce via card_codingFunction_of_card_supports.
nodes.statement: Again, we apply \cref{prop:card_codingFunction_of_card_supports}.
nodes.name: Reduce via card_codingFunction_of_card_supports

nodes.statement_short: Orbits via card_supportOrbit and the bottom case.
nodes.statement: The first claim follows from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit}, where this time we use the fact that there are less than \( \#\mu \) \( \bot \)-coding functions (\cref{prop:card_codingFunction_bot}).
nodes.name: Orbits via card_supportOrbit and the bottom case

nodes.statement_short: Supported sets via card_supports_atoms and coherent data.
nodes.statement: The second claim follows from \cref{prop:card_supports_atoms} to \( \bot \)-extensions of type \( \beta \) objects, noting that \( \beta \)-supports correspond to base supports and that \( \beta \)-allowable permutations correspond to base permutations.\footnote{One useful claim to prove for this is that there is a unique path \( \beta \tpath \bot \), and so type \( \beta \) objects satisfy \( \bot \)-extensionality by injectivity of \( U_\beta \).} The fact that \( \beta \)-allowable permutations correspond to base permutations relies on the fact that we can construct a \( \beta \)-permutation from a base permutation using coherent data (\cref{def:CoherentData}).
nodes.name: Supported sets via card_supports_atoms and coherent data

nodes.statement: Suppose that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions. Then if \( \gamma < \beta \) is a proper type index, there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \) \( (\gamma,\beta) \)-raised singletons.
nodes.name: card_raisedSingleton
assumptions: Suppose that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions.
\( \gamma < \beta \) is a proper type index
conclusions: there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \) \( (\gamma,\beta) \)-raised singletons
nodes.label: prop:card_raisedSingleton

nodes.statement: A \( (\gamma,\beta) \)-raised singleton \( \rsing(S,u) = \chi_{(\singleton_\beta(u), S + \dsupp(u)^\beta)} \) is determined by a triple \( (R, o, \chi) \) where \begin{itemize} \item \( R \) is the \( \beta \)-tree given by \( R_A = i \) when \( S_A = (i, f) \); \item \( o \) is the support orbit of \( S + \dsupp(u)^\beta \); and \item \( \chi \) is the coding function \( \chi_{(u, \dsupp(u))} \). \end{itemize} Indeed, suppose \( \rsing(S, u) \) and \( \rsing(T, v) \) have the same triple \( (R, o, \chi) \). We must show that \[ \chi_{(\singleton_\beta(u), S + \dsupp(u)^\beta)} = \chi_{(\singleton_\beta(v), S + \dsupp(v)^\beta)} \] Then there is a \( \beta \)-allowable \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(S + \dsupp(u)^\beta) = T + \dsupp(v)^\beta \), and as they have the same tree \( R \), we can decompose this into \( \rho(S) = T \) and \( \rho(\dsupp(u)^\beta) = \dsupp(v)^\beta \). In particular, \( \rho_\beta(\dsupp(u)) = \dsupp(v) \). As \( \chi_{(u, \dsupp(u))} = \chi_{(v, \dsupp(v))} \), there is a \( \gamma \)-allowable permutation \( \rho' \) such that \( \rho'(u) = v \) and \( \rho'(\dsupp(u)) = \dsupp(v) \). Hence \( \rho_\beta(u) = v \). This gives \[ \rho(\singleton_\beta(u)) = \singleton_\beta(\rho_\beta(u)) = \singleton_\beta(v) \] as required. Now, it remains to show that there are less than \( \#\mu \) such triples \( (R, o, \chi) \). But this follows directly from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit} and the assumption on the cardinalities of the types of coding functions.
nodes.name: Proof of card_raisedSingleton
nodes.statement_short: Encode a raised singleton by a triple (R, o, chi), show the encoding is injective, and count triples.
Define the triple.

nodes.name: Same triple: show equal raised singletons

nodes.statement_short: Decompose rho using the tree R.
nodes.statement: Then there is a \( \beta \)-allowable \( \rho \) such that \( \rho(S + \dsupp(u)^\beta) = T + \dsupp(v)^\beta \), and as they have the same tree \( R \), we can decompose this into \( \rho(S) = T \) and \( \rho(\dsupp(u)^\beta) = \dsupp(v)^\beta \). In particular, \( \rho_\beta(\dsupp(u)) = \dsupp(v) \).
nodes.name: Decompose rho using the tree R

nodes.statement_short: Equal coding functions give rho_beta(u) = v.
nodes.statement: As \( \chi_{(u, \dsupp(u))} = \chi_{(v, \dsupp(v))} \), there is a \( \gamma \)-allowable permutation \( \rho' \) such that \( \rho'(u) = v \) and \( \rho'(\dsupp(u)) = \dsupp(v) \). Hence \( \rho_\beta(u) = v \).
nodes.name: Equal coding functions give rho_beta(u) = v

nodes.statement_short: rho maps the singletons.
nodes.statement: This gives \[ \rho(\singleton_\beta(u)) = \singleton_\beta(\rho_\beta(u)) = \singleton_\beta(v) \] as required.
nodes.name: rho maps the singletons

nodes.statement_short: Count the triples.
nodes.statement: Now, it remains to show that there are less than \( \#\mu \) such triples \( (R, o, \chi) \). But this follows directly from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit} and the assumption on the cardinalities of the types of coding functions.
nodes.name: Count the triples

nodes.statement: There are less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \beta \)-coding functions for all type indices \( \beta \leq \alpha \).
nodes.name: card_codingFunction
nodes.statement_short: There are fewer than #mu coding functions at every level up to alpha.
conclusions: There are less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \beta \)-coding functions for all type indices \( \beta \leq \alpha \).
nodes.label: prop:card_codingFunction

nodes.statement: By induction we may assume that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions. By \cref{prop:card_codingFunction_bot,prop:card_codingFunction_min}, we may assume that \( \beta \) is a proper type index, and that it is not minimal in \( \lambda \), so there is some proper type index \( \gamma < \beta \). By \cref{prop:recode}, every \( \beta \)-coding function is determined by a set of \( (\gamma,\beta) \)-raised singletons \( s \) and support orbit \( o \). The conclusion then follows from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit,prop:card_raisedSingleton} and the fact that \( \#\mu \) is a strong limit.
nodes.name: Proof of card_codingFunction
nodes.statement_short: Induction on beta; base cases handled separately; recode via raised singletons and count.
Assume the bound below beta.
nodes.statement: By induction we may assume that for all type indices \( \delta < \beta \), there are strictly less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \delta \)-coding functions.
nodes.name: Assume the bound below beta

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to non-minimal proper beta.
nodes.statement: By \cref{prop:card_codingFunction_bot,prop:card_codingFunction_min}, we may assume that \( \beta \) is a proper type index, and that it is not minimal in \( \lambda \), so there is some proper type index \( \gamma < \beta \).
nodes.name: Reduce to non-minimal proper beta

nodes.statement_short: Recode via raised singletons.
nodes.statement: By \cref{prop:recode}, every \( \beta \)-coding function is determined by a set of \( (\gamma,\beta) \)-raised singletons \( s \) and support orbit \( o \).
nodes.name: Recode via raised singletons

nodes.statement_short: Count via orbits, raised singletons and strong limit.
nodes.statement: The conclusion then follows from \cref{prop:card_supportOrbit,prop:card_raisedSingleton} and the fact that \( \#\mu \) is a strong limit.
nodes.name: Count via orbits, raised singletons and strong limit

nodes.statement: For each type index \( \beta \leq \alpha \), \( \#\TSet_\beta = \#\mu \).
nodes.name: card_tSet
nodes.statement_short: Each level of t-sets has exactly #mu elements.
assumptions: For each type index \( \beta \leq \alpha \)
conclusions: \( \#\TSet_\beta = \#\mu \)
nodes.label: prop:card_tSet

nodes.statement: If \( \beta \) is \( \bot \), we already know \( \#\TSet_\bot = \#\Atom = \#\mu \), so suppose \( \#\beta \) is a proper type index. Each object \( x : \TSet_\beta \) is determined by a \( \beta \)-coding function and a \( \beta \)-support. Since there are less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \beta \)-coding functions (\cref{prop:card_codingFunction}) and there are exactly \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-supports, we obtain \( \#\TSet_\beta \leq \#\mu \). Since the typed near-litter map \( \NearLitter \to \TSet_\beta \) is injective, there are at least \( \#\NearLitter = \#\mu \) inhabitants of \( \TSet_\beta \), giving the result by antisymmetry.
nodes.name: Proof of card_tSet
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound from coding functions and supports; lower bound from typed near-litters.
Bottom case known.
nodes.statement: If \( \beta \) is \( \bot \), we already know \( \#\TSet_\bot = \#\Atom = \#\mu \), so suppose \( \#\beta \) is a proper type index.
nodes.name: Bottom case known

nodes.statement_short: Each t-set is determined by a coding function and support.
nodes.statement: Each object \( x : \TSet_\beta \) is determined by a \( \beta \)-coding function and a \( \beta \)-support.
nodes.name: Each t-set is determined by a coding function and support

nodes.statement_short: Upper bound.
nodes.statement: Since there are less than \( \#\mu \)-many \( \beta \)-coding functions (\cref{prop:card_codingFunction}) and there are exactly \( \#\mu \) \( \beta \)-supports, we obtain \( \#\TSet_\beta \leq \#\mu \).
nodes.name: Upper bound

nodes.statement_short: Lower bound; antisymmetry.
nodes.statement: Since the typed near-litter map \( \NearLitter \to \TSet_\beta \) is injective, there are at least \( \#\NearLitter = \#\mu \) inhabitants of \( \TSet_\beta \), giving the result by antisymmetry.
nodes.name: Lower bound; antisymmetry

nodes.statement: For each type index \( \beta \leq \alpha \), \( \#\Tang_\beta = \#\mu \).
nodes.name: card_tangle
assumptions: For each type index \( \beta \leq \alpha \)
conclusions: \( \#\Tang_\beta = \#\mu \)
nodes.label: prop:card_tangle

nodes.statement: Use \cref{prop:card_tSet} and the fact that there are precisely \( \#\mu \)-many \( \beta \)-supports.
nodes.name: Proof of card_tangle
nodes.statement_short: From card_tSet and the count of supports.

nodes.statement: Let \( I : \Type_u \) be a type with a well-founded transitive relation \( \prec \). Let \( A : I \to \Type_v \) be a family of types indexed by \( I \), and let \[ B : \prod_{i : I} A_i \to \left(\prod_{j : I} j \prec i \to A_j\right) \to \Sort_w \] An \emph{inductive construction} for \( (I, A, B) \) is a pair of functions \begin{align*} &F_A : \prod_{i : I} \prod_{d : \prod_{j : I} j \prec i \to A_j} \\ &\quad\left( \prod_{j : I} \prod_{h : j \prec i} B\ j\ (d\ j\ h)\ (k\ h' \mapsto d\ k\ (\newoperator{trans}(h',h))) \right) \to A_i \\ &F_B : \prod_{i : I} \prod_{d : \prod_{j : I} j \prec i \to A_j} \\ &\quad\prod_{h : \left( \prod_{j : I} \prod_{h : j \prec i} B\ j\ (d\ j\ h)\ (k\ h' \mapsto d\ k\ (\newoperator{trans}(h',h))) \right)} B\ i\ (F_A\ i\ d\ h)\ d \end{align*}
nodes.name: inductive construction
nodes.statement_short: An inductive construction: functions building data A_i and hypotheses B_i from data and hypotheses below i.
nodes.label: def:IC

nodes.statement: Let \( (F_A, F_B) \) be an inductive construction for \( (I, A, B) \), where \( w \) is \( 0 \). Then there are computable functions \[ G : \prod_{i : I} A_i;\quad H : \prod_{i : I} B\ i\ G_i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto G_j) \] such that for each \( i : I \), \[ G_i = F_A\ i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto G_j)\ (F_B\ i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto H_j)) \]
nodes.name: inductive construction theorem for propositions
nodes.statement_short: An inductive construction with propositional hypotheses has a computable fixed point.
assumptions: Let \( (F_A, F_B) \) be an inductive construction for \( (I, A, B) \), where \( w \) is \( 0 \).
conclusions: there are computable functions \[ G : \prod_{i : I} A_i;\quad H : \prod_{i : I} B\ i\ G_i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto G_j) \] such that for each \( i : I \), \[ G_i = F_A\ i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto G_j)\ (F_B\ i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto H_j)) \]
nodes.label: prop:IC.fix_prop

nodes.statement:
Recall that \( \Part \alpha \) denotes the type \( \sum_{p: \Prop} (p 	o \alpha) \). For \( i : I \), we define the \emph{hypothesis} on data \( t : \prod_{j : I} j \prec i 	o \Part A_j \) to be the proposition  egin{align*} 
ewoperator{IH}(i, t) = &\sum_{D : \prod_{j : I} \prod_{h : j \prec i} \pr_1(t\ j\ h)} \prod_{j : I} \prod_{h : j \prec i} B\ j\ (\pr_2(t\ j\ h)\ (D\ j\ h))\ &\quad(k\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(t\ k\ (
ewoperator{trans}(h',h)))\ (D\ k\ (
ewoperator{trans}(h',h))))) \end{align*} Now we define \( K : \prod_{i : I} \Part A_i \) by \[ K = 
ewoperator{fix}_{\Part A_{(-)}} \left( i t \mapsto \left\langle 
ewoperator{IH}(i, t), h \mapsto F_A\ i\ (j\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(t\ j\ h')\ (\pr_1(h)\ j\ h')))\ \pr_2(h) ightangle ight) \] where \( 
ewoperator{fix}_C \) is the fixed point function for \( \prec \) and induction motive \( C : I 	o \Type_v \), with type \[ 
ewoperator{fix}_C : \left( \prod_{i : I} \left( \prod_{j : I} j \prec i 	o C_j ight) 	o C_i ight) 	o \prod_{i : I} C_i \] By definition of \( 
ewoperator{fix} \), we obtain the equation \[ K_i = \left\langle 
ewoperator{IH}(i, j \_ \mapsto K_j), h \mapsto F_A\ i\ (j\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(K_j)\ (\pr_1(h)\ j\ h')))\ \pr_2(h) ightangle \] Further, if \( h_1 : \pr_1(K_i) \), we have the equation \[ \pr_2(K_i)\ h_1 = F_A\ i\ (j\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(K_j)\ (\pr_1(h_2)\ j\ h')))\ \pr_2(h_2) \] where \( h_2 : 
ewoperator{IH}(i, j \_ \mapsto K_j) \) is obtained by casting from \( h_1 \) using the previous equation; this equation is derived from the extensionality principle of \( \Part \), which states that \[ \prod_{x, y : \Part \alpha} \left( \prod_{a : \alpha} (\exists h,\, a = \pr_2(x)\ h) \leftrightarrow (\exists h,\, a = \pr_2(y)\ h) ight) x = y \] Using these two equations, we may now show directly by induction on \( i \) that \( D' : \prod_{i : I} \pr_1(K_i) \). ootnote{TODO: More details?} From this, we may define \( G : \prod_{i : I} A_i \) by \( G_i = \pr_2(K_i)\ D'_i \). We may then easily obtain \( H : \prod_{i : I}\ B\ i\ G_i\ (j \_ \mapsto G_j) \) by appealing to \( F_B \) and the two equations above. The required equality also easily follows from the two given equations.
nodes.name: Proof of inductive construction theorem for propositions
nodes.statement_short: Define a partial fixed point K carrying the induction hypothesis as a proposition, prove by induction that it is always defined, and extract G and H.
Recall Part.
nodes.statement: Recall that \( \Part \alpha \) denotes the type \( \sum_{p: \Prop} (p \to \alpha) \).

nodes.statement_short: Define the hypothesis IH.

nodes.statement_short: Define K via the fixed point.
nodes.statement:
Now we define \( K : \prod_{i : I} \Part A_i \) by \[ K = 
ewoperator{fix}_{\Part A_{(-)}} \left( i t \mapsto \left\langle 
ewoperator{IH}(i, t), h \mapsto F_A\ i\ (j\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(t\ j\ h')\ (\pr_1(h)\ j\ h')))\ \pr_2(h) ightangle ight) \] where \( 
ewoperator{fix}_C \) is the fixed point function for \( \prec \) and induction motive \( C : I 	o \Type_v \), with type \[ 
ewoperator{fix}_C : \left( \prod_{i : I} \left( \prod_{j : I} j \prec i 	o C_j ight) 	o C_i ight) 	o \prod_{i : I} C_i \]
nodes.name: Define K via the fixed point

nodes.statement_short: Unfolding equation for K.
nodes.statement: By definition of \( \newoperator{fix} \), we obtain the equation \[ K_i = \left\langle \newoperator{IH}(i, j \_ \mapsto K_j), h \mapsto F_A\ i\ (j\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(K_j)\ (\pr_1(h)\ j\ h')))\ \pr_2(h) \right\rangle \]
nodes.name: Unfolding equation for K

nodes.statement_short: Second equation via Part extensionality.
nodes.statement: Further, if \( h_1 : \pr_1(K_i) \), we have the equation \[ \pr_2(K_i)\ h_1 = F_A\ i\ (j\ h' \mapsto (\pr_2(K_j)\ (\pr_1(h_2)\ j\ h')))\ \pr_2(h_2) \] where \( h_2 : \newoperator{IH}(i, j \_ \mapsto K_j) \) is obtained by casting from \( h_1 \) using the previous equation; this equation is derived from the extensionality principle of \( \Part \), which states that \[ \prod_{x, y : \Part \alpha} \left( \prod_{a : \alpha} (\exists h,\, a = \pr_2(x)\ h) \leftrightarrow (\exists h,\, a = \pr_2(y)\ h) \right) x = y \]
nodes.name: Second equation via Part extensionality

nodes.statement_short: K is always defined, by induction.
nodes.statement: Using these two equations, we may now show directly by induction on \( i \) that \( D' : \prod_{i : I} \pr_1(K_i) \).\footnote{TODO: More details?}
nodes.name: K is always defined, by induction

nodes.statement_short: Define G and H and check the equation.
nodes.statement: From this, we may define \( G : \prod_{i : I} A_i \) by \( G_i = \pr_2(K_i)\ D'_i \). We may then easily obtain \( H : \prod_{i : I}\ B\ i\ G_i\ (j \_ \mapsto G_j) \) by appealing to \( F_B \) and the two equations above. The required equality also easily follows from the two given equations.

nodes.statement: Let \( (F_A, F_B) \) be an inductive construction for \( (I, A, B) \). nodes.name: inductive construction theorem
nodes.statement_short: Every inductive construction has a noncomputable fixed point.
assumptions: Let \( (F_A, F_B) \) be an inductive construction for \( (I, A, B) \).
conclusions: there are \emph{noncomputable} functions \[ G : \prod_{i : I} A_i;\quad H : \prod_{i : I} B\ i\ G_i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto G_j) \] such that for each \( i : I \), \[ G_i = F_A\ i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto G_j)\ (F_B\ i\ (j\ \_ \mapsto H_j)) \]

nodes.statement:
Define \[ C : \prod_{i : I} A_i 	o \left(\prod_{j : I} j \prec i 	o A_jight) 	o \Prop \] by \( C\ i\ x\ d = 
ewoperator{Nonempty}(B\ i\ x\ d) \). We then define the inductive construction \( (F_A', F_B') \) for \( (I, A, C) \) by \[ F_A'\ i\ d\ h = F_A\ i\ d\ (j h' \mapsto 
ewoperator{some}(h\ j\ h'));\quad F_B'\ i\ d\ h = \langle F_B\ i\ d\ (j h' \mapsto 
ewoperator{some}(h\ j\ h')) angle \] where \( \langle-angle \) is the constructor and \( 
ewoperator{some} \) is the noncomputable destructor of \( 
ewoperator{Nonempty} \). The result is then direct from \cref{prop:IC.fix_prop}.

Truncate B to a proposition C.
nodes.statement: Define \[ C : \prod_{i : I} A_i \to \left(\prod_{j : I} j \prec i \to A_j\right) \to \Prop \] by \( C\ i\ x\ d = \newoperator{Nonempty}(B\ i\ x\ d) \).

nodes.statement_short: Lift the construction using some.
nodes.statement:
We then define the inductive construction \( (F_A', F_B') \) for \( (I, A, C) \) by \[ F_A'\ i\ d\ h = F_A\ i\ d\ (j h' \mapsto 
ewoperator{some}(h\ j\ h'));\quad F_B'\ i\ d\ h = \langle F_B\ i\ d\ (j h' \mapsto 
ewoperator{some}(h\ j\ h')) angle \] where \( \langle-angle \) is the constructor and \( 
ewoperator{some} \) is the noncomputable destructor of \( 
ewoperator{Nonempty} \).

nodes.statement: The result is then direct from \cref{prop:IC.fix_prop}.
nodes.name: Apply IC.fix_prop

nodes.statement: For a proper type index \( \alpha \), the \emph{main motive} at \( \alpha \) is the type \( \Motive_\alpha \) consisting of model data at \( \alpha \), a position function for \( \Tang_\alpha \), and typed near-litters at \( \alpha \), such that if \( (x, S) \) is an \( \alpha \)-tangle and \( y \) is an atom or near-litter that occurs in the range of \( S_A \), then \( \iota(y) < \iota(x, S) \).
nodes.name: main motive
nodes.label: def:MainMotive

nodes.statement: We define the \emph{main hypothesis} \[ \Hypothesis : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \Motive_\alpha \to \left( \prod_{\beta < \alpha} \Motive_\beta \right) \to \Type_{u+1} \] at \( \alpha \), given \( \Motive_\alpha \) and \( \prod_{\beta < \alpha} \Motive_\beta \), to be the type consisting of the following data. \begin{itemize} \item For \( \gamma < \beta \leq \alpha \), there is a map \( \AllPerm_\beta \to \AllPerm_\gamma \) that commutes with the coercions from \( \AllPerm_{(-)} \) to \( \StrPerm_{(-)} \). \item Let \( \beta, \gamma < \alpha \) be distinct with \( \gamma \) proper. Let \( t : \Tang_\beta \) and \( \rho : \AllPerm_\alpha \). Then \[ (\rho_\gamma)_\bot(f_{\beta,\gamma}(t)) = f_{\beta,\gamma}(\rho_\beta(t)) \] \item Suppose that \( (\rho(\beta))_{\beta < \alpha} \) is a collection of allowable permutations such that whenever \( \beta, \gamma < \alpha \) are distinct, \( \gamma \) is proper, and \( t : \Tang_\gamma \), we have \[ (\rho(\gamma))_\bot(f_{\beta,\gamma}(t)) = f_{\beta,\gamma}(\rho(\beta)(t)) \] Then there is an \( \alpha \)-allowable permutation \( \rho \) with \( \rho_\beta = \rho(\beta) \) for each \( \beta < \alpha \). \item For any \( \beta < \alpha \), \[ U_\alpha(x)(\beta) \subseteq \ran U_\beta \] \item (extensionality) If \( \beta : \lambda \) is such that \( \beta < \alpha \), the map \( U_\alpha(-)(\beta) : \TSet_\beta \to \Set \StrSet_\beta \) is injective. \item If \( \beta : \lambda \) is such that \( \beta < \alpha \), for every \( x : \TSet_\beta \) there is some \( y : \TSet_\alpha \) such that \( U_\alpha(y)(\beta) = \{ x \} \), and we write \( \singleton_\alpha(x) \) for this object \( y \). \end{itemize}
nodes.name: main hypothesis
nodes.statement_short: The main hypothesis: coherence conditions relating the motive at alpha to those below.
nodes.label: def:MainHypothesis

nodes.statement: The \emph{inductive step for the main motive} is the function \begin{align*} &\newoperator{Step}_M : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \prod_{M : \prod_{\beta < \alpha} \Motive_\beta} \\ &\quad\left( \prod_{\beta : \lambda} \prod_{h : \beta < \alpha} \Hypothesis\ \beta\ (M\ \beta\ h)\ (\gamma\ h' \mapsto M\ \gamma\ (\newoperator{trans}(h',h))) \right) \to \Motive_\alpha \end{align*} given as follows. Given the hypotheses \( \alpha, M, H \), we use \cref{def:NewModelData} to construct model data at level \( \alpha \). Then, combine this with \( H \) to create an instance of coherent data below level \( \alpha \).\footnote{This requires using the definition of new allowable permutations. There may be some difficulties here in converting between the types of model data at level \( \alpha \) together with model data at all \( \beta < \alpha \), and model data at all levels \( \beta \leq \alpha \).} By \cref{prop:card_tangle}, we conclude that \( \#\Tang_\alpha = \#\mu \), and so by \cref{prop:newPos} there is a position function on \( \Tang_\alpha \) that respects the typed near-litters defined in \cref{def:newTypedNearLitter}. These data comprise the main motive at level \( \alpha \).
nodes.name: inductive step for the main motive
nodes.statement_short: Build the main motive at alpha from model data, coherence, the cardinality bound and new positions.
nodes.label: def:motiveStep

nodes.statement:
The \emph{inductive step for the main hypothesis} is the function  egin{align*} &
ewoperator{Step}_H : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \prod_{M : \prod_{ eta < \alpha} \Motive_ eta} \ &\quad\prod_{H : \prod_{ eta : \lambda} \prod_{h :  eta < \alpha} \Hypothesis\  eta\ (M\  eta\ h)\ (\gamma\ h' \mapsto M\ \gamma\ (
ewoperator{trans}(h',h)))}\ &\quad\Hypothesis\ \alpha\ (
ewoperator{Step}_M\ \alpha\ M\ H)\ M \end{align*} given as follows. Given the hypotheses \( \alpha, M, H \), we use the definitions from \cref{def:motiveStep} to obtain model data at level \( \alpha \) and coherent data below level \( \alpha \). The remaining proof obligations are handled by \cref{def:newSingleton,prop:newPos}.
nodes.name: inductive step for the main hypothesis
nodes.label: def:hypothesisStep

nodes.statement:
There are noncomputable functions \[ 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive} : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \Motive_\alpha \] and \[ 
ewoperator{ComputeHypothesis} : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \Hypothesis\ \alpha\ 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_\alpha\ ( eta\ \_ \mapsto 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_ eta) \] such that for each \( \alpha : \lambda \),  egin{align*} 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_\alpha = &
ewoperator{Step}_M\ \alpha\ ( eta\ \_ \mapsto 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_ eta)\ &(
ewoperator{Step}_H\ \alpha\ ( eta\ \_ \mapsto 
ewoperator{ComputeHypothesis}_ eta)) \end{align*}
nodes.name: model construction
nodes.statement_short: The main motive and hypothesis can be computed at every proper type index by the inductive construction.
conclusions:
There are noncomputable functions \[ 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive} : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \Motive_\alpha \] and \[ 
ewoperator{ComputeHypothesis} : \prod_{\alpha : \lambda} \Hypothesis\ \alpha\ 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_\alpha\ ( eta\ \_ \mapsto 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_ eta) \] such that for each \( \alpha : \lambda \),  egin{align*} 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_\alpha = &
ewoperator{Step}_M\ \alpha\ ( eta\ \_ \mapsto 
ewoperator{ComputeMotive}_ eta)\ &(
ewoperator{Step}_H\ \alpha\ ( eta\ \_ \mapsto 
ewoperator{ComputeHypothesis}_ eta)) \end{align*}

nodes.statement: Direct from \cref{prop:IC.fix}.

nodes.statement: We can then reconstruct, for each level \( \alpha \), the type of coherent data below \( \alpha \).
nodes.name: reconstructing coherent data

nodes.statement: In this section, let \( \gamma < \beta \) be proper type indices strictly below the current level \( \alpha \).
nodes.name: levels for raising strong supports

nodes.statement: Let \( T \) be a \( \gamma \)-support, and let \( U \) be the strong support generated by \( T^\beta \). If \( A \) is a path such that \( \im U_A^\NearLitter \) is nonempty, then \( A \) has length at least 2.
nodes.name: raiseStrong_length
assumptions: Let \( T \) be a \( \gamma \)-support, and let \( U \) be the strong support generated by \( T^\beta \).
\( A \) is a path such that \( \im U_A^\NearLitter \) is nonempty
conclusions: \( A \) has length at least 2
nodes.label: prop:raiseStrong_length

nodes.statement: Let \( N \in \im U_A^\NearLitter \). Either \( A \) is of the form \( B^\beta \) for \( B : \gamma \tpath \bot \) and \( N \in \im T_B^\NearLitter \), in which case \( B \) clearly has length at least 2 as \( \gamma \) is a proper type index, or \( N \in \im V_B^\NearLitter \) where \( A = B^\beta \) and \( B : \delta \tpath \bot \), and \( V \) supports some \( \delta \)-set. But we cannot have \( \delta = \bot \), because \( \bot \)-supports that support some \( \delta \)-set cannot contain near-litters, so in this other case \( A \) also has length at least 2.
nodes.name: Proof of raiseStrong_length
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on where a near-litter of the generated strong support comes from.
Either from T or from an inflexible closure step.
nodes.statement: Let \( N \in \im U_A^\NearLitter \). Either \( A \) is of the form \( B^\beta \) for \( B : \gamma \tpath \bot \) and \( N \in \im T_B^\NearLitter \), in which case \( B \) clearly has length at least 2 as \( \gamma \) is a proper type index, or \( N \in \im V_B^\NearLitter \) where \( A = B^\beta \) and \( B : \delta \tpath \bot \), and \( V \) supports some \( \delta \)-set.
nodes.name: Either from T or from an inflexible closure step

nodes.statement_short: Bottom supports have no near-litters, so length at least 2.
nodes.statement: But we cannot have \( \delta = \bot \), because \( \bot \)-supports that support some \( \delta \)-set cannot contain near-litters, so in this other case \( A \) also has length at least 2.
nodes.name: Bottom supports have no near-litters, so length at least 2

nodes.statement: Let \( T \) be a \( \gamma \)-support, and let \( U \) be the strong support generated by \( T^\beta \). Then \( U^\alpha \) is strong.
nodes.name: raiseStrong
assumptions: Let \( T \) be a \( \gamma \)-support, and let \( U \) be the strong support generated by \( T^\beta \).
conclusions: \( U^\alpha \) is strong
nodes.label: prop:raiseStrong

nodes.statement: The interference condition is clear. First we show that proofs that \( A^\alpha \)-inflexibility for litters that appear in \( U^\alpha \) correspond to proofs of \( A \)-inflexibility. Clearly if \( L \) is \( A^\alpha \)-flexible then \( L \) is \( A \)-flexible. Instead, let \( I = (\delta, \varepsilon, \zeta, A) \) be an inflexible \( \alpha \)-path and \( t : \Tang_\varepsilon \) such that there is a near-litter \( N \in \im (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{{A_\zeta}_\bot} \) with \( N^\circ = f_{\varepsilon,\zeta}(t) \). Suppose that \( A \) is the empty path, so \( \delta = \alpha \). Then \( (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{{A_\zeta}_\bot} = (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{\zeta_\bot} \) is nonempty, so \( \zeta = \beta \). This shows that \( \im (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{\beta_\bot} = \im U^\NearLitter_\bot \) is nonempty, contradicting \cref{prop:raiseStrong_length}. So \( A \) is nonempty, and is of the form \( B^\alpha \) for \( B : \beta \tpath \delta \). So \( (\delta,\varepsilon,\zeta,B) \) is an inflexible \( \beta \)-path for \( N^\circ \). The expected conclusion then follows directly from the fact that \( U \) is strong.
nodes.name: Proof of raiseStrong
nodes.statement_short: Show inflexibility proofs for raised paths reduce to the unraised ones, ruling out the empty path via raiseStrong_length; then use strength of U.
Inflexible paths for U^alpha correspond to paths for U.
nodes.statement: The interference condition is clear. First we show that proofs that \( A^\alpha \)-inflexibility for litters that appear in \( U^\alpha \) correspond to proofs of \( A \)-inflexibility. Clearly if \( L \) is \( A^\alpha \)-flexible then \( L \) is \( A \)-flexible. Instead, let \( I = (\delta, \varepsilon, \zeta, A) \) be an inflexible \( \alpha \)-path and \( t : \Tang_\varepsilon \) such that there is a near-litter \( N \in \im (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{{A_\zeta}_\bot} \) with \( N^\circ = f_{\varepsilon,\zeta}(t) \). Suppose that \( A \) is the empty path, so \( \delta = \alpha \). Then \( (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{{A_\zeta}_\bot} = (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{\zeta_\bot} \) is nonempty, so \( \zeta = \beta \). This shows that \( \im (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{\beta_\bot} = \im U^\NearLitter_\bot \) is nonempty, contradicting \cref{prop:raiseStrong_length}. nodes.statement_short: Flexible case direct; take an inflexible alpha-path.
nodes.statement: Clearly if \( L \) is \( A^\alpha \)-flexible then \( L \) is \( A \)-flexible. Instead, let \( I = (\delta, \varepsilon, \zeta, A) \) be an inflexible \( \alpha \)-path and \( t : \Tang_\varepsilon \) such that there is a near-litter \( N \in \im (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{{A_\zeta}_\bot} \) with \( N^\circ = f_{\varepsilon,\zeta}(t) \).
nodes.name: Flexible case direct; take an inflexible alpha-path

nodes.statement_short: Empty path contradicts raiseStrong_length.
nodes.statement: Suppose that \( A \) is the empty path, so \( \delta = \alpha \). Then \( (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{{A_\zeta}_\bot} = (U^\alpha)^\NearLitter_{\zeta_\bot} \) is nonempty, so \( \zeta = \beta \). nodes.statement_short: So the path is raised from a beta-path.
nodes.statement: So \( A \) is nonempty, and is of the form \( B^\alpha \) for \( B : \beta \tpath \delta \). So \( (\delta,\varepsilon,\zeta,B) \) is an inflexible \( \beta \)-path for \( N^\circ \).
nodes.name: So the path is raised from a beta-path

nodes.statement_short: Strength of U gives the result.
nodes.statement: The expected conclusion then follows directly from the fact that \( U \) is strong.
nodes.name: Strength of U gives the result

nodes.statement: Let \( S \) be a strong \( \alpha \)-support and let \( T \) be a \( \gamma \)-support. Let \( U \) be the strong support generated by \( T^\beta \), and let \( V \) be the support whose image is precisely those atoms in the interference of \( S_\beta \) and \( U \). Let \( \rho \) be a \( \beta \)-allowable permutation that fixes \( S_\beta \). Then \( S + (\rho(U + V))^\alpha \) is strong.
nodes.name: raiseRaise_strong
assumptions: Let \( S \) be a strong \( \alpha \)-support and let \( T \) be a \( \gamma \)-support.
Let \( U \) be the strong support generated by \( T^\beta \), and let \( V \) be the support whose image is precisely those atoms in the interference of \( S_\beta \) and \( U \).
Let \( \rho \) be a \( \beta \)-allowable permutation that fixes \( S_\beta \).
conclusions: \( S + (\rho(U + V))^\alpha \) is strong
nodes.label: prop:raiseRaise_strong

nodes.statement: Follows directly from \cref{prop:Strong.smul,prop:raiseStrong}.
nodes.name: Proof of raiseRaise_strong
nodes.statement_short: Combine Strong.smul and raiseStrong.

nodes.statement: Let \( S \) be a strong \( \alpha \)-support. Let \( U \) be a strong \( \beta \)-support with the property that if \( A \) is a path such that \( \im U_A^\NearLitter \) is nonempty, then \( A \) has length at least 2. Then for every \( \beta \)-allowable \( \rho \) that fixes \( S_\beta \), we have \( \spec(S + U^\alpha) = \spec(S + (\rho(U))^\alpha) \).
nodes.name: combineStrong
assumptions: Let \( S \) be a strong \( \alpha \)-support.
Let \( U \) be a strong \( \beta \)-support with the property that if \( A \) is a path such that \( \im U_A^\NearLitter \) is nonempty, then \( A \) has length at least 2.
conclusions: for every \( \beta \)-allowable \( \rho \) that fixes \( S_\beta \), we have \( \spec(S + U^\alpha) = \spec(S + (\rho(U))^\alpha) \)
nodes.label: prop:combineStrong

nodes.statement: Appeal to \cref{prop:spec_eq_spec_iff}. First, note that \( (i, a) \in (S + (\rho(U))^\alpha)_A^\Atom \) if and only if \( (i, a) \in S \) or \( A = B^\alpha \) and \( (i, a) \in \rho(U)_B^\Atom \). Thus, \begin{align*} (i, a_1) \in (S + U^\alpha)_A^\Atom &\to \exists a_2,\, (i, a_2) \in (S + (\rho(U))^\alpha)_A^\Atom \\ &\quad\wedge [(\exists B,\, A = B^\alpha \wedge \rho_B(a_1) = a_2) \vee ((\forall B,\, A \neq B^\alpha) \wedge a_1 = a_2)] \end{align*} and the same holds for the other direction\footnote{We can prove the other direction easily from this by substituting \( \rho(U) \) and \( \rho^{-1} \).} and for near-litters. The coimage condition is clear. Suppose that \( (i, a_1) \in (S + U^\alpha)_A^\Atom \) and \( (i, a_2) \in (S + (\rho(U))^\alpha)_A^\Atom \). Then by coinjectivity we can apply the above result, giving that either there is \( B \) such that \( A = B^\alpha \) and \( \rho_B(a_1) = a_2 \), or there is no such \( B \), and \( a_1 = a_2 \). In either case, the result is easy to show. The result for litters follows from the fact that the condition on \( U \) implies that proofs of inflexiblity of litters in \( U \) correspond bijectively to proofs of inflexibility of litters in \( U^\alpha \).\footnote{TODO: Probably want more details when we get here.}
nodes.name: Proof of combineStrong

nodes.statement: Let \( \beta < \alpha \) be proper type indices. A set \( s : \TSet_\beta \) is called \emph{\( \alpha \)-symmetric} if there is some \( \alpha \)-support \( S \) such that if \( \rho \) is an \( \alpha \)-allowable permutation that fixes \( S \), then \( \rho \) fixes \( s \) setwise. Note that it suffices to prove that for all \( \rho \) that fix \( S \), \( s \subseteq \rho[s] \) (or alternatively, \( \rho[s] \subseteq s \)). Every small set is symmetric, since a support can be obtained by raising the types of chosen supports for elements of the set and then collating the results.
nodes.name: symmetric
nodes.label: def:Symmetric

nodes.statement: Let \( \beta < \alpha \) be proper type indices. Let \( s : \TSet_\beta \) be \( \alpha \)-symmetric. Then there is \( x : \TSet_\alpha \) such that \[ \forall y : \TSet_\beta,\, y \in_\beta^\alpha x \leftrightarrow y \in s \] Moreover, every \( x : \TSet_\alpha \) arises in this way; this is an induction principle for \( \TSet_\alpha \).
nodes.name: TSet.of_symmetric
assumptions: Let \( \beta < \alpha \) be proper type indices.
Let \( s : \TSet_\beta \) be \( \alpha \)-symmetric.
conclusions: there is \( x : \TSet_\alpha \) such that \[ \forall y : \TSet_\beta,\, y \in_\beta^\alpha x \leftrightarrow y \in s \]
every \( x : \TSet_\alpha \) arises in this way

nodes.statement: If \( s \) is empty, the result follows directly from the definition of \( \TSet_\alpha \). Otherwise, consider the code \( (\beta, s) \). By \cref{def:Code.Represents}, there is exactly one code \( d \) such that \( c \looparrowright (\beta, s) \). Then \( c \) is a new t-set at level \( \alpha \), so is naturally an inhabitant of \( \TSet_\alpha \). Using the membership relation from \cref{prop:Code.ext}, the type-\( \beta \) members of \( c \) are precisely \( s \), as required. For the induction principle, we apply the above construction to the set \[ s = \{ y \mid y \in^\alpha_\beta x \} \] and use extensionality to deduce that the object constructed is exactly \( x \).
nodes.name: Proof of TSet.of_symmetric

nodes.statement: Let \( \gamma < \beta < \alpha \) be proper type indices. Let \( s : \Set \TSet_\gamma \) be such that \( \singleton_\beta[s] \) is \( \alpha \)-symmetric. Then \( s \) is \( \beta \)-symmetric.
nodes.name: unions of singletons
assumptions: Let \( \gamma < \beta < \alpha \) be proper type indices.
Let \( s : \Set \TSet_\gamma \) be such that \( \singleton_\beta[s] \) is \( \alpha \)-symmetric.
conclusions: \( s \) is \( \beta \)-symmetric
nodes.label: prop:singleton_union

nodes.statement: Let \( S \) be an \( \alpha \)-support for \( \singleton_\beta[s] \), which without loss of generality is strong. We claim that the \( \alpha \)-symmetry of \( s \) is witnessed by \( S_\beta \). Let \( \rho \) be a \( \beta \)-allowable permutation such that \( \rho(S_\beta) = S_\beta \). Let \( x \in s \); it suffices by substituting \( \rho^{-1} \) to prove that \( \rho_\gamma(x) \in s \). As \( x : \TSet_\gamma \), there is a \( \gamma \)-support \( T \) for \( x \). By \cref{prop:exists_allowable_of_fixes}, there is an \( \alpha \)-allowable permutation \( \rho' \) such that \[ \rho'(S) = S;\quad (\rho'_\beta)_\gamma(T) = \rho_\gamma(T) \] Thus, \[ \rho'_\beta(\singleton_\beta[s]) = \singleton_\beta[s];\quad (\rho'_\beta)_\gamma(x) = \rho_\gamma(x) \] We thus have \begin{align*} x &\in s \\ \singleton_\beta(x) &\in \singleton_\beta[s] \\ \rho'_\beta(\singleton_\beta(x)) &\in \rho'_\beta(\singleton_\beta[s]) \\ \rho'_\beta(\singleton_\beta(x)) &\in \singleton_\beta[s] \\ \singleton_\beta((\rho'_\beta)_\gamma(x)) &\in \singleton_\beta[s] \\ \singleton_\beta(\rho_\gamma(x)) &\in \singleton_\beta[s] \\ \rho_\gamma(x) &\in s \\ \end{align*}
nodes.name: Proof of unions of singletons
nodes.statement_short: Witness beta-symmetry by S_beta: lift a beta-permutation fixing S_beta to an alpha-permutation fixing S, then chase singletons.
Take a strong support S; S_beta witnesses symmetry of s.

nodes.statement: Let \( \{ x \}_\beta \) be an abbreviation for \( \singleton_\beta(x) \), and let \( \langle x, y \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \) be an abbreviation for \( \{ \{ x \}_\gamma, \{ x, y \}_\gamma \}_\beta \). Then, the following axioms hold for our model \( \TSet \) at all sequences of proper type indices \( \zeta < \varepsilon < \delta < \gamma < \beta < \alpha \). \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{llcl} \( - \) & extensionality & \( \forall x^\alpha,\, \forall y^\alpha,\, (\forall z^\beta,\, z \in x \leftrightarrow z \in y) \to x = y \) \\ P1(a) & intersection & \( \forall x^\alpha y^\alpha,\, \exists z^\alpha,\, \forall w^\beta,\, w \in z \leftrightarrow (w \in x \wedge w \in y) \) \\ P1(b) & complement & \( \forall x^\alpha,\, \exists z^\alpha,\, \forall w^\beta,\, w \in z \leftrightarrow w \notin x \) \\ \( - \) & singleton & \( \forall x^\beta,\, \exists y^\alpha,\, \forall z^\beta,\, z \in y \leftrightarrow z = x \) \\ P2 & singleton image & \( \forall x^\beta,\, \exists y^\alpha,\, \forall z^\varepsilon w^\varepsilon,\, \langle \{ z \}_\delta, \{ w \}_\delta \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in y \leftrightarrow \langle z, w \rangle_{\delta,\gamma} \in x \) \\ P3 & insertion two & \( \forall x^\gamma,\, \exists y^\alpha,\, \forall z^\zeta w^\zeta t^\zeta,\, \langle \{ \{ z \}_\varepsilon \}_\delta, \langle w, t \rangle_{\varepsilon, \delta} \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in y \leftrightarrow \langle z, t \rangle_{\varepsilon,\delta} \in x \) \\ P4 & insertion three & \( \forall x^\gamma,\, \exists y^\alpha,\, \forall z^\zeta w^\zeta t^\zeta,\, \langle \{ \{ z \}_\varepsilon \}_\delta, \langle w, t \rangle_{\varepsilon,\delta} \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in y \leftrightarrow \langle z, w \rangle_{\varepsilon,\delta} \in x \) \\ P5 & cross product & \( \forall x^\gamma,\, \exists y^\alpha,\, \forall z^\beta,\, z \in y \leftrightarrow \exists w^\delta t^\delta,\, z = \langle w, t \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \wedge t \in x \) \\ P6 & type lowering & \( \forall x^\alpha,\, \exists y^\delta,\, \forall z^\varepsilon,\, z \in y \leftrightarrow \forall w^\delta,\, \langle w, \{ z \}_\delta \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in x \) \\ P7 & converse & \( \forall x^\alpha,\, \exists y^\alpha,\, \forall z^\delta w^\delta,\, \langle z, w \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in y \leftrightarrow \langle w, z \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in x \) \\ P8 & cardinal one & \( \exists x^\alpha,\, \forall y^\beta,\, y \in x \leftrightarrow \exists z^\gamma,\, \forall w,\, w \in y \leftrightarrow w = z \) \\ P9 & subset & \( \exists x^\alpha,\, \forall y^\delta z^\delta,\, \langle y, z \rangle_{\gamma,\beta} \in x \leftrightarrow \forall w^\varepsilon,\, w \in y \to w \in z \) \end{tabular} \end{center}
nodes.name: consistency of tangled type theory

nodes.statement: A \emph{\( \Sigma \)-language} consists of a map \( \newoperator{Functions} : \prod_{n : \mathbb N} (\Fin n \to \Sigma) \to \Sigma \to \Type_u \) and a map \( \newoperator{Relations} : \prod_{n : \mathbb N} (\Fin n \to \Sigma) \to \Type_v \).
nodes.name: Sigma-language
Phi-morphism of languages

nodes.statement:
Let \( L, L' \) be \( \Sigma \)-languages. We define \( L \oplus L' \) to be the \( \Sigma \)-language with \[ 
ewoperator{Functions}(n, A, B) = 
ewoperator{Functions}_L(n, A, B) \oplus 
ewoperator{Functions}_{L'}(n, A, B) \] and \[ 
ewoperator{Relations}(n, A) = 
ewoperator{Relations}_L(n, A) \oplus 
ewoperator{Relations}_{L'}(n, A) \] There are morphisms of languages \( L, L' 	o L \oplus L' \).
nodes.name: sum of languages

nodes.statement:
Let \( L \) be a \( \Sigma \)-language, and let \( M : \Sigma 	o \Type_w \). An \emph{\( L \)-structure} on \( M \) consists of a map \[ 
ewoperator{funMap} : \prod_{n : \mathbb N} \prod_{A : \Fin n 	o \Sigma} \prod_{B : \Sigma} 
ewoperator{Functions}(n, A, B) 	o \left(\prod_{i : \Fin n} M(A(i)) ight) 	o M(B) \] and a map \[ 
ewoperator{relMap} : \prod_{n : \mathbb N} \prod_{A : \Fin n 	o \Sigma} 
ewoperator{Relations}(n, A) 	o \left(\prod_{i : \Fin n} M(A(i)) ight) 	o \Prop \] We will write \( f^M \) for \( 
ewoperator{funMap}(n, A, B, f) \), and similarly \( R^M \) for \( 
ewoperator{relMap}(n, R) \). If \( M \) is an \( L \)-structure and an \( L' \)-structure, it is also naturally an \( (L \oplus L') \)-structure. If \( M \) is an \( L \)-structure and an \( L' \)-structure, then a morphism of \( \Sigma \)-languages \( \Phi : L 	o L' \) is called an \emph{expansion} on \( M \) if it commutes with the interpretations of all symbols on \( M \).
nodes.name: L-structure

nodes.statement: Let \( L \) be a \( \Sigma \)-language. A \emph{morphism} of \( L \)-structures \( M \to N \) consists of functions \( h_A : M_A \to N_A \) such that for all \( n : \mathbb N \), \( A : \Fin n \to \Sigma \), and \( B : \Sigma \), all function symbols \( f : \newoperator{Functions}(n, A, B) \), and all \( x : \prod_{i : \Fin n} M(A(i)) \), \[ h_B(f^M(x)) = f^N(i \mapsto h_{A(i)}(x(i))) \] and for all relation symbols \( R : \newoperator{Relations}(n, A) \), \[ R^M(x) \to R^N(i \mapsto h_{A(i)}(x(i))) \]
nodes.name: morphism of L-structures

nodes.statement: Let \( L \) be a \( \Sigma \)-language, and let \( \alpha : \Type_{u'} \) be a sort of variables of sort \( S : \alpha \to \Sigma \). An \emph{\( L \)-term on \( \alpha : S \) of sort \( A \)}, the type of which is denoted \( \Term_{\alpha:S} A \), is either \begin{itemize} \item a variable, comprised solely of a name \( n : \alpha \) such that \( S(n) = A \), or \item an application of a function symbol, comprised of some \( n : \mathbb N \), a map \( B : \Fin n \to \Sigma \), a function symbol \( f : \newoperator{Functions}(n, B, A) \), and terms \( t : \prod_{i : \Fin n} \Term_{\alpha:S} B(i) \). \end{itemize}
nodes.name: L-term

nodes.statement:
Let \( L \) be a \( \Sigma \)-language, and let \( \alpha : \Type_{u'} \) and \( S : \alpha 	o \Sigma \). We define the type of \emph{\( L \)-bounded formulae on \( \alpha : S \)} with free variables indexed by \( \alpha \), and \( n \) additional free variables of sorts \( f : \Fin n 	o \Sigma \), denoted \( \BForm_{\alpha:S}^f \), by the following constructors.  egin{itemize} \item \(

nodes.name: L-bounded formula
nodes.statement_short: Bounded formulae of a many-sorted language, built from falsum, equality, relations, implication and universal quantification.

nodes.statement: Let \( L \) be a \( \Sigma \)-language. A \emph{1-\( L \)-formula} of sort \( A \) is an \( L \)-bounded formula on \( \newoperator{Empty} \) with one additional free variable of sort \( f : \Fin 1 \to \Sigma \) given by \( f(x) = A \).
nodes.name: 1-L-formula

nodes.statement: Let \( L \) be a \( \Sigma \)-language. The \emph{witness symbols} for \( L \) is the language \( L_W \) consisting of a single constant of sort \( A \) for every 1-\( L \)-formula of sort \( A \).
nodes.name: witness symbols

nodes.statement: Let \( M \) be a nonempty \( L \)-structure. Then \( M \) has an \( L_W \)-structure such that for each 1-\( L \)-formula \( \phi \) of sort \( A \), there is a constant symbol \( c : \newoperator{Functions}(0, \#[], A) \) such that \[ \forall x : M_A,\, \phi(x) \to \phi(c) \]
nodes.name: witness structure
assumptions: Let \( M \) be a nonempty \( L \)-structure.
conclusions: \( M \) has an \( L_W \)-structure such that for each 1-\( L \)-formula \( \phi \) of sort \( A \), there is a constant symbol \( c : \newoperator{Functions}(0, \#[], A) \) such that \[ \forall x : M_A,\, \phi(x) \to \phi(c) \]

nodes.statement: We define the interpretation of the constant for \( \phi \) to be some \( x : M \) such that \( M \vDash \phi(x) \) if one exists, or an arbitrary \( y : M \) otherwise.\footnote{Use mathlib's \texttt{Classical.epsilon}.} This defines an \( L_W \)-structure for \( M \), and clearly \( M \) satisfies the required property.
nodes.name: Proof of witness structure
nodes.statement_short: Interpret each witness constant by a choice of witness.

nodes.statement: For each \( n : \mathbb N \), we define \[ L^{(0)} = L;\quad L^{(n+1)} = L^{(n)} \oplus (L^{(n)})_W \] This forms a directed diagram of languages, which has a colimit \( L^{(\omega)} \). There are natural morphisms \( L \to L^{(\omega)} \) and \( L^{(n)} \to L^{(\omega)} \) which are expansions on \( M \).
nodes.name: iterated witness language

nodes.statement: Let \( M \) be a nonempty \( L \)-structure. Then \( M \) has an \( L^{(\omega)} \)-structure such that for each 1-\( L^{(\omega)} \)-formula \( \phi \) of sort \( A \), there is a constant symbol \( c : \newoperator{Functions}(0, \#[], A) \) such that \[ \forall x : M_A,\, \phi(x) \to \phi(c) \] Then, by the Tarski--Vaught test (which must be proven in the many-sorted case), the set \( N \subseteq M \) comprised of all of the interpretations of \( L^{(\omega)} \)-terms, is the domain of an \( L^{(\omega)} \)-elementary substructure of \( M \).
nodes.name: term model is an elementary substructure
assumptions: Let \( M \) be a nonempty \( L \)-structure.
conclusions: \( M \) has an \( L^{(\omega)} \)-structure such that for each 1-\( L^{(\omega)} \)-formula \( \phi \) of sort \( A \), there is a constant symbol \( c : \newoperator{Functions}(0, \#[], A) \) such that \[ \forall x : M_A,\, \phi(x) \to \phi(c) \] Then, by the Tarski--Vaught test (which must be proven in the many-sorted case), the set \( N \subseteq M \) comprised of all of the interpretations of \( L^{(\omega)} \)-terms, is the domain of an \( L^{(\omega)} \)-elementary substructure of \( M \).

nodes.statement: Let \( L \) be an \( \mathbb N \)-language. A \emph{type raising morphism} is a map of languages \( L \xrightarrow{\newoperator{succ}} L \), where \( \newoperator{succ} : \mathbb N \to \mathbb N \) is the successor function.
nodes.name: type raising morphism

nodes.statement: Let \( R : \sigma \to \tau \to \Prop \). We define \begin{itemize} \item the \emph{image} of \( R \) to be the set \( \im R = \{ y : \tau \mid \exists x : \sigma,\, x \mathrel{R} y \} \); \item the \emph{coimage} of \( R \) to be the set \( \coim R = \{ x : \sigma \mid \exists y : \tau,\, x \mathrel{R} y \} \) (note that this is \emph{not} the same as the category-theoretic coimage of a morphism); \item the \emph{field} of \( R \) to be the set \( \field R = \coim R \cup \im R \); \item the \emph{image of \( R \) on} \( s : \Set \sigma \) to be the set \( \im R|_s = \{ y : \tau \mid \exists x \in s,\, x \mathrel{R} y \} \); \item the \emph{coimage of \( R \) on} \( t : \Set \tau \) to be the set \( \coim R|_t = \{ x : \sigma \mid \exists y \in t,\, x \mathrel{R} y \} \); \item the \emph{converse} of \( R \) to be the relation \( R^{-1} : \tau \to \sigma \to \Prop \) such that \( y \mathrel{R^{-1}} x \) if and only if \( x \mathrel{R} y \); \item if \( S : \tau \to \upsilon \to \Prop \), the \emph{composition} \( S \circ R : \sigma \to \upsilon \to \Prop \) is the relation given by \( x \mathrel{(S\circ R)} z \) if and only if there is \( y : \tau \) such that \( x \mathrel{R} y \) and \( y \mathrel{S} z \); \item for a natural number \( n \), the \emph{\( n \)th power} of \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) is defined by \( R^{n+1} = R \circ R^n \) and \( R^0 \) is the identity relation on \( \coim R \); \item for an integer \( n \), the \emph{\( n \)th power} of \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) is defined by \( R^{(n : \mathbb Z)} = R^n \) and \( R^{-(n : \mathbb Z)} = (R^n)^{-1} \) for \( n : \mathbb N \).\footnote{This may be implemented using \texttt{Int.negInduction} from mathlib.} \end{itemize} We say that \( R \) is \begin{itemize} \item \emph{injective}, if \( s_1 \mathrel{R} t, s_2 \mathrel{R} t \) imply \( s_1 = s_2 \); \item \emph{surjective}, if for every \( t : \tau \), there is some \( s : \sigma \) such that \( s \mathrel{R} t \); \item \emph{coinjective}, if \( s \mathrel{R} t_1, s \mathrel{R} t_2 \) imply \( t_1 = t_2 \); \item \emph{cosurjective}, if for every \( s : \sigma \), there is some \( t : \tau \) such that \( s \mathrel{R} t \); \item \emph{functional}, if \( R \) is coinjective and cosurjective, or equivalently, for every \( s : \sigma \) there is exactly one \( t : \tau \) such that \( s \mathrel{R} t \); \item \emph{cofunctional}, if \( R \) is injective and surjective, or equivalently, for every \( t : \tau \) there is exactly one \( s : \sigma \) such that \( s \mathrel{R} t \); \item \emph{one-to-one}, if \( R \) is injective and coinjective; \item \emph{bijective}, if \( R \) is functional and cofunctional; \item \emph{permutative}, if \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) is one-to-one and has equal image and coimage. \end{itemize} We also define the \emph{graph} of a function \( f : \sigma \to \tau \) to be the functional relation \( R : \sigma \to \tau \to \Prop \) given by \( (x, y) \in R \) if and only if \( f(x) = y \). Most of these definitions are from \url{https://www.kylem.net/math/relations.html}, and most of these are in mathlib under \texttt{Mathlib.Logic.Relator}.
nodes.name: properties of relations
nodes.statement_short: Image, coimage, field, converse, composition, powers and injectivity-type properties of relations.
nodes.label: def:relation_props

nodes.statement: \mbox\negthinspace \begin{enumerate} \item \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) is permutative if and only if it is one-to-one and for all \( x : \tau \), there exists \( y \) such that \( x \mathrel{R} y \) if and only if there exists \( y \) such that \( y \mathrel{R} x \). \item If \( R, S : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) are permutative and \( \coim R \cap \coim S = \emptyset \), then \( R \sqcup S \) is permutative and has coimage \( \coim R \cup \coim S \). \item If \( R, S : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) are permutative and \( \coim R = \coim S \), then \( R \circ S \) is permutative and has coimage equal to that of \( R \) and \( S \). \item If \( R \) is permutative, then \( \coim R^n = \coim R = \im R = \im R^n \) for any natural number or integer \( n \). \item If \( R \) is permutative and \( s_1, s_2 \subseteq \coim R \), then the image of \( R \) on \( s_1 \) is equal to \( s_2 \) if and only if the coimage of \( R \) on \( s_2 \) is equal to \( s_1 \). \end{enumerate}
nodes.name: results on relations
nodes.statement_short: Basic facts about permutative relations: unions, compositions, powers and images.
conclusions: \mbox\negthinspace \begin{enumerate} \item \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) is permutative if and only if it is one-to-one and for all \( x : \tau \), there exists \( y \) such that \( x \mathrel{R} y \) if and only if there exists \( y \) such that \( y \mathrel{R} x \). \item If \( R, S : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) are permutative and \( \coim R \cap \coim S = \emptyset \), then \( R \sqcup S \) is permutative and has coimage \( \coim R \cup \coim S \). \item If \( R, S : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) are permutative and \( \coim R = \coim S \), then \( R \circ S \) is permutative and has coimage equal to that of \( R \) and \( S \). \item If \( R \) is permutative, then \( \coim R^n = \coim R = \im R = \im R^n \) for any natural number or integer \( n \). \item If \( R \) is permutative and \( s_1, s_2 \subseteq \coim R \), then the image of \( R \) on \( s_1 \) is equal to \( s_2 \) if and only if the coimage of \( R \) on \( s_2 \) is equal to \( s_1 \). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: prop:relation_results

nodes.statement: Let \( s : \Set \tau \). An \emph{orbit restriction} for \( s \) (over some type \( \sigma \)) consists of a set \( t : \Set \tau \) disjoint from \( s \), a function \( f : \tau \to \sigma \), and a permutation \( \pi : \sigma \simeq \sigma \), such that for each \( u : \sigma \), the set \( t \cap f^{-1}(u) \) has cardinality at least \( \max(\aleph_0, \#s, \#d) \). An orbit restriction encapsulates information about how orbits should be completed. \begin{itemize} \item \( t \) is the \emph{sandbox}, the set inside which all added items must reside. \item \( f \) is a \emph{categorisation function}, placing each value \( x : \tau \) into a category \( u : \sigma \). \item \( \pi \) is a permutation of categories. If \( x \) has category \( u \), then anything that \( x \) is mapped to should have category \( \pi(u) \). \end{itemize}
nodes.name: orbit restriction
nodes.label: def:OrbitRestriction

nodes.statement: Let \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) be a one-to-one relation, and let \( (t, f, \pi) \) be an orbit restriction for \( \field R \) over some type \( \sigma \). Then there is a permutative relation \( T \) such that \begin{itemize} \item \( \coim T \subseteq \field R \cup t \); \item \( \#\coim T \leq \max(\aleph_0, \#\coim R) \); \item \( R \leq T \); and \item if \( (x, y) \in T \), then \( (x, y) \in R \vee f(y) = \pi(f(x)) \). \end{itemize}
nodes.name: completing restricted orbits
nodes.statement_short: A one-to-one relation can be completed to a permutative relation using a sandbox respecting category permutations.
assumptions: Let \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) be a one-to-one relation, and let \( (t, f, \pi) \) be an orbit restriction for \( \field R \) over some type \( \sigma \).
conclusions: there is a permutative relation \( T \) such that \begin{itemize} \item \( \coim T \subseteq \field R \cup t \); \item \( \#\coim T \leq \max(\aleph_0, \#\coim R) \); \item \( R \leq T \); and \item if \( (x, y) \in T \), then \( (x, y) \in R \vee f(y) = \pi(f(x)) \). \end{itemize}
nodes.label: prop:completing_restricted_orbits

nodes.statement: For each \( u : \sigma \), define an injection \( i_u : \field R \times \mathbb N \to \tau \) where \( \im i_u \subseteq t \cap f^{-1}(u) \). Define a relation \( S \) on \( \tau \) by the following constructors. \begin{align*} \forall x \in \coim R \setminus \im R,\, &(i_{\pi^{-1}(f(x))}(x, 0), x) \in S \\ \forall n : \mathbb N,\, \forall x \in \coim R \setminus \im R,\, &(i_{\pi^{-n-2}(x)}(x, n+1), i_{\pi^{-n-1}(x)}(x, n)) \in S \\ \forall x \in \im R \setminus \coim R,\, &(x, i_{\pi(f(x))}(x, 0)) \in S \\ \forall n : \mathbb N,\, \forall x \in \im R \setminus \coim R,\, &(i_{\pi^{n+1}(f(x))}(x, n), i_{\pi^{n+2}(f(x))}(x, n+1)) \in S \end{align*} Note that \( (x, y) \in S \) implies \( f(y) = \pi(f(x)) \). Finally, as \( R \sqcup S \) is permutative, it satisfies the required conclusion.
nodes.name: Proof of completing restricted orbits
nodes.statement_short: Extend each open chain of R by fresh elements from the sandbox in the prescribed categories.
Define injections into the sandbox and the relation S.
nodes.statement: For each \( u : \sigma \), define an injection \( i_u : \field R \times \mathbb N \to \tau \) where \( \im i_u \subseteq t \cap f^{-1}(u) \). Define a relation \( S \) on \( \tau \) by the following constructors. \begin{align*} \forall x \in \coim R \setminus \im R,\, &(i_{\pi^{-1}(f(x))}(x, 0), x) \in S \\ \forall n : \mathbb N,\, \forall x \in \coim R \setminus \im R,\, &(i_{\pi^{-n-2}(x)}(x, n+1), i_{\pi^{-n-1}(x)}(x, n)) \in S \\ \forall x \in \im R \setminus \coim R,\, &(x, i_{\pi(f(x))}(x, 0)) \in S \\ \forall n : \mathbb N,\, \forall x \in \im R \setminus \coim R,\, &(i_{\pi^{n+1}(f(x))}(x, n), i_{\pi^{n+2}(f(x))}(x, n+1)) \in S \end{align*}
nodes.name: Define injections into the sandbox and the relation S

nodes.statement_short: S respects categories.
nodes.statement: Note that \( (x, y) \in S \) implies \( f(y) = \pi(f(x)) \).
nodes.name: S respects categories

nodes.statement_short: R union S is permutative.
nodes.statement: Finally, as \( R \sqcup S \) is permutative, it satisfies the required conclusion.
nodes.name: R union S is permutative

nodes.statement: Let \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) be a one-to-one relation. Let \( s : \Set \tau \) be an infinite set such that \( \#\field R \leq \#s \), and \( \field R \) and \( s \) are disjoint. Then there is a permutative relation \( S \) such that \( R \leq S \) and \( \coim S \subseteq \field R \cup s \).
nodes.name: completing orbits
assumptions: Let \( R : \tau \to \tau \to \Prop \) be a one-to-one relation.
Let \( s : \Set \tau \) be an infinite set such that \( \#\field R \leq \#s \), and \( \field R \) and \( s \) are disjoint.
conclusions: there is a permutative relation \( S \) such that \( R \leq S \) and \( \coim S \subseteq \field R \cup s \)

nodes.statement: Define the orbit restriction \( (s, f, \pi) \) for \( \field R \) over \( \Unit \). Note that for this to be defined, we used the inequality \[ \#s \geq \max(\aleph_0, \#\field R) \] Use \cref{prop:completing_restricted_orbits} to obtain a permutative relation \( T \) extending \( R \) defined on \( \field R \cup s \).

Small subsets are bounded.
